headline: Medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risks arise from ACI’s broad egress and Pipecat’s shared-bus, multi-service defaults.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: aci can ingest external content through APIs, email, Slack, Notion, and MCP-style tool use, while pipecat runs on a shared bus and can pass conversation state across instances. That creates a plausible default pathway for attacker-controlled text from A to influence B’s downstream prompts or handlers. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes severity upward.
conditions: IF aci forwards untrusted email/Slack/Notion content into prompts or MCP calls
IF pipecat consumes shared-bus conversation state without provenance filtering
mitigations: Add a provenance tag to all ACI-fed text before it reaches Pipecat
Disable automatic prompt construction from email/Slack/Notion content
Insert a human review step for any shared-bus message containing instructions
requires-engineering: enforce content-type separation between data and instructions
requires-engineering: add allowlisted message schemas on the shared bus

B_data_leakage.rationale: aci touches CRM, email, calendar, support, and research data and has broad network egress; pipecat touches text, conversation state, audio/video, and can call many third-party STT/LLM/TTS services. In a shared-workflow pair, sensitive data can flow from A into B and then out to external APIs. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so this is inferred rather than directly observed.
conditions: IF aci passes CRM/email/calendar content into pipecat transcripts or prompts
IF pipecat is configured with any third-party STT/LLM/TTS provider
mitigations: Restrict ACI inputs to redacted fields only
Turn off third-party transcription or LLM providers in Pipecat
Use a local-only test tenant for both agents
requires-engineering: add DLP filtering before any outbound API call
requires-engineering: segregate sensitive and non-sensitive workflows

C_capability_conflict.rationale: aci supports multiple instances and broad API writes to business systems, while pipecat explicitly shares state on a bus across instances. Even without a shared filesystem, overlapping mutable state and concurrent instances can race on conversation or CRM-adjacent workflows. Because no locking is documented, the safer choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same downstream record or conversation thread
IF the orchestrator does not provide per-session locking
mitigations: Assign one writer per resource type
Serialize writes through a single queue
Pause one agent during critical updates
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks
requires-engineering: partition shared state by session ID

D_cascading_error.rationale: aci can generate CRM/email/calendar actions from research and support data, and pipecat can route text through LLM and transport services. If Pipecat treats ACI output as authoritative, a mistaken or manipulated ACI result can cascade into spoken or API-driven actions. The downstream blast radius includes external communications, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF pipecat forwards ACI-produced text into an action-taking LLM or transport
IF no verification step checks ACI outputs before execution
mitigations: Require a verification prompt before any action
Show ACI outputs to an operator before execution
Limit Pipecat to read-only summarization
requires-engineering: add structured validation for ACI outputs
requires-engineering: block direct action execution from untrusted text

E_compliance.rationale: aci handles customer support, CRM, email, and secrets management, while pipecat processes audio, video, text, and conversation state and can send data to many external providers. That creates a plausible compliance mismatch for retention, residency, or subject-rights handling, even though no specific jurisdiction is documented. Uncertainty keeps this at medium, not low.
conditions: IF regulated customer data is routed from aci into Pipecat cloud providers
IF retention or deletion policies differ across the two systems
mitigations: Classify data before routing it between agents
Keep regulated records out of Pipecat providers
Document retention and deletion settings for both systems
requires-engineering: add jurisdiction-aware routing
requires-engineering: implement per-field retention controls
